t: Autograd: the dynamic graph, gradients, no_grad and custom functions
sum: How PyTorch records a graph while your forward pass runs and walks it backwards: leaf tensors, grad_fn, .grad accumulation, saved tensors, retain_graph, no_grad vs inference_mode, detach, hooks, higher-order gradients and writing your own autograd.Function.
prereq: dl1
Backpropagation is the chain rule applied over a computation graph from the loss backwards: each node multiplies the incoming gradient by its local derivative and passes it to its inputs.
mc13
A tiny autograd engine stores, for each value, its parents and a closure that computes local gradients; backward sorts the graph topologically and accumulates gradients with +=.
pt1
Tensors carry a version counter that in-place ops bump; autograd refuses to use a saved tensor whose version changed. Leaf tensors that require grad cannot be modified in place.
why:
In the NumPy implementations of this app (mc11, mc13) you wrote backward passes by hand: for every layer, a function that takes the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer's output and returns the gradients with respect to its inputs and weights, plus the bookkeeping to keep the forward values those formulas need. That is fine for a two-layer network. For a transformer with rotary embeddings, grouped-query attention, a mixture-of-experts router and a custom loss, hand-written backward code would be thousands of lines, and every change to the forward pass would need a matching change to the backward pass — the perfect breeding ground for gradient bugs that do not crash but quietly make the model worse.

PyTorch's autograd removes that work. You write only the forward pass in ordinary Python, and PyTorch records what you did and differentiates it. It feels like magic, which is exactly why engineers who only know the surface get stuck when it misbehaves: gradients that double every step because nobody zeroed them, memory that explodes during evaluation because a graph was still being recorded, "Trying to backward through the graph a second time" in a recurrent model, NaN gradients from a forward pass that contains no NaN, a frozen layer that keeps moving, or an intermediate tensor whose .grad is mysteriously None.

In ML-debugging interviews, autograd questions sort candidates quickly. "Why is the evaluation loop out of memory?" "Why does this RNN crash on the second batch?" "Why is this gradient NaN?" Each has a crisp answer if you know what the engine records, when it frees things, and which flags change its behaviour.

This lesson opens the box. It starts from what happens on every operation when a tensor requires gradients, traces a backward pass by hand with real numbers, and then covers the rules you need in practice: leaves and accumulation, saved tensors and retain_graph, the three ways to turn tracking off (no_grad, inference_mode, detach) and how they differ, non-scalar outputs and vector–Jacobian products, hooks, higher-order gradients, and writing and testing your own torch.autograd.Function. It finishes with the NaN-gradient traps and the anomaly detector that finds them.
primer:
Think of autograd as a flight recorder. When the forward pass runs, every operation that touches a tensor marked requires_grad=True writes an entry: "I was a multiplication; my inputs came from these two places; to compute my gradients later I will need these two values, so I have kept them". Each entry is a node, and each node points back to the nodes that produced its inputs. When you call loss.backward(), PyTorch plays the recording in reverse, starting at the loss: each node takes the gradient arriving from above, applies its local derivative rule using the values it kept, and passes the results to the nodes it points to. When the playback reaches a tensor you created yourself — a parameter — it adds the result into that tensor's .grad.

Four facts fall out of that picture:

  • The graph is rebuilt every forward pass. The recording is made while your Python runs, so loops, ifs and recursion simply produce whatever graph they produced this time. This is the "dynamic" or "define-by-run" graph.
  • Recording costs memory. The values nodes keep — saved tensors — are mostly activations, and they are the main memory cost of training. They are released as the backward playback passes each node.
  • Gradients accumulate. The playback adds into .grad; it never overwrites. Clearing them is your job.
  • You can switch the recorder off. Inside torch.no_grad() nothing is recorded, which is what evaluation and parameter updates need.

It helps to hold a rough cost model from the start, because most autograd questions in interviews are really cost questions. The forward pass does the work you wrote. The backward pass does roughly twice that work in arithmetic, because for every matrix multiplication in the forward it needs two — one for the gradient with respect to the input, one for the gradient with respect to the weight. Memory is dominated not by the graph's nodes, which are small objects, but by the saved tensors those nodes hold: for a transformer that means the inputs of every linear layer, the attention probabilities or their compact substitutes, the outputs of activations and normalisations. Weights and their gradients have a fixed size; saved activations grow with batch size and sequence length. So when someone asks "why is this using so much memory?" the first suspect is "what is autograd keeping alive, and for how long?", and when someone asks "how do I make evaluation cheaper?" the first answer is "stop recording".

It also helps to know what autograd is not. It is not symbolic differentiation: it never produces a formula for the derivative, only numbers for this particular input. It is not numerical differentiation either: no small perturbations, no finite-difference error — each node applies an exact derivative rule. It is reverse-mode automatic differentiation by operator overloading: the PyTorch paper (Paszke et al., NeurIPS 2019) describes it as building "a representation of the computed function every time it is executed", chosen because Python is too dynamic for ahead-of-time source transformation.

Where the flight-recorder analogy breaks: a real recorder captures everything, while autograd records only operations whose inputs require gradients — operations on plain data tensors are not recorded at all, which is why loading data costs no graph memory. And a real recorder can be replayed many times; autograd's playback discards what it has used, so by default you get one backward pass per forward.

If you remember one sentence: the forward pass builds a graph of nodes that keep what their derivative needs; backward replays it once, in reverse, adding into the leaves' .grad, and freeing as it goes.
body:
1. requires_grad and how it spreads

Every tensor has a flag, requires_grad. Parameters created by nn.Module layers have it set to True; data tensors do not. The rule for results is simple: the output of an operation requires grad if any of its inputs does (and recording is enabled). So w * x requires grad because w does, even though x is data.

x = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
w = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
b = torch.tensor(1.0, requires_grad=True)
y = w * x + b       # requires_grad=True, grad_fn=<AddBackward0>
z = y.relu()        # grad_fn=<ReluBackward0>
L = z ** 2          # grad_fn=<PowBackward0>

Each result has a grad_fn: the graph node that produced it. The node points to the nodes of its inputs through next_functions; on 2.14 L.grad_fn.next_functions is ((<ReluBackward0>, 0),). Following those links from the loss visits the whole graph. A leaf that requires grad appears in the graph as an AccumulateGrad node, whose only job is to add the arriving gradient into the leaf's .grad.

2. Leaf and non-leaf tensors

A leaf tensor is one that autograd did not compute: you created it, or it is a parameter. x.is_leaf is True; y.is_leaf is False. A tensor that does not require grad is also a leaf, trivially. The distinction matters because:

  • Only leaves that require grad receive .grad after backward. For an intermediate such as y, y.grad is None and 2.14 warns that "The .grad attribute of a Tensor that is not a leaf Tensor is being accessed". If you need it, call y.retain_grad() before backward.
  • Leaves that require grad cannot be modified in place outside no_grad (pt1), because their identity is what .grad refers to.
  • Operations such as .to(device) or .float() on a leaf produce a non-leaf. A common bug: w = torch.randn(3, requires_grad=True).cuda() creates a leaf on the CPU and a non-leaf copy on the GPU; the model uses the copy, the optimiser holds the copy, and .grad on it is always None. Create tensors on the right device directly — torch.randn(3, device="cuda", requires_grad=True) — or use nn.Parameter inside a module and move the module.

3. Running backward by hand

Calling L.backward() on the graph above (checked on 2.14):

  1. Start with dL/dL = 1.
  2. PowBackward (L = z²) saved z = 7; it returns 1 · 2z = 14 for z.
  3. ReluBackward saved its output; since the output is positive it passes 14 through (it would pass 0 where the output is 0).
  4. AddBackward (y = (w·x) + b) has local derivative 1 for both inputs: it sends 14 to the Mul node and 14 to b's AccumulateGrad. b.grad = 14.
  5. MulBackward saved w and x; it returns 14 · x = 28 for w and 14 · w = 42 for x. w.grad = 28, x.grad = 42.

The engine visits nodes in an order where each node runs only after all gradients flowing into it have arrived (a reverse topological order), so a tensor used twice — a residual connection, a shared embedding — gets the sum of the gradients from both uses before its node runs. That summing is the chain rule's "add over paths", done for you.

4. What each node computes: vector–Jacobian products

For a function from n inputs to m outputs, the Jacobian J is the m × n matrix of partial derivatives. The chain rule says the gradient of a scalar loss with respect to the inputs is v · J, where v is the gradient with respect to the outputs. That product is a vector–Jacobian product (VJP), and it is what every backward node computes — without ever building J. For an element-wise ReLU over a million elements, J would be a million × million diagonal matrix; the VJP is just "multiply v by 1 where the output was positive, 0 elsewhere". For a matmul Y = X W, the VJPs are dX = dY Wᵀ and dW = Xᵀ dY, two matmuls of the same size as the forward. This is why a backward pass costs about twice the forward in FLOPs: each matmul in the forward becomes two in the backward.

It also explains an error you will see: (v * 2).backward() on a 3-element output raises "grad can be implicitly created only for scalar outputs". For a scalar loss, v is simply 1; for a vector output PyTorch does not know which v you want. Pass one explicitly — out.backward(torch.ones_like(out)) gives the gradient of out.sum() — or reduce to a scalar first. If you truly need the full Jacobian, that is one VJP per output row; torch.func.jacrev does it with vmap.

5. Accumulation into .grad

AccumulateGrad adds. Run this on 2.14:

w = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
for _ in range(3):
    (w * 2).backward()
w.grad    # tensor(6.)  — 2 + 2 + 2

This is a feature. Gradient accumulation — running several small batches and stepping once — is just "call backward k times, then step", because the gradients sum. (Each micro-batch loss must be divided by k to get the average; pt6 shows the bug when it is not.) It also means every training loop must clear gradients once per optimiser step. optimizer.zero_grad() and model.zero_grad() both default to set_to_none=True on 2.14, which sets .grad = None instead of filling it with zeros: cheaper, and the next backward allocates fresh. Code that reads p.grad after zero_grad must handle None.

6. Saved tensors, freeing, and retain_graph

Each node saves what its backward formula needs: exp saves its result (d/dx eˣ = eˣ), sigmoid its output, mul both inputs, a linear layer its input (to compute dW = Xᵀ dY). On 2.14 you can peek: a.exp().grad_fn._saved_result. These saved tensors are the activations whose memory dominates training (pt7 does the arithmetic: for a transformer they often exceed the weights many times over).

To keep memory down, backward frees each node's saved tensors as soon as it has used them. Calling backward again on the same graph then fails:

RuntimeError: Trying to backward through the graph a second time (or directly
access saved tensors after they have already been freed). Saved intermediate
values of the graph are freed when you call .backward() or autograd.grad().
Specify retain_graph=True if you need to backward through the graph a second time ...

Two situations produce it. The legitimate one: two losses that share part of a forward pass and are backpropagated separately; pass retain_graph=True to the first backward (or, better, sum the losses and backpropagate once). The common bug: a tensor kept across iterations still references the previous iteration's graph — an RNN hidden state carried from batch to batch, a running "memory" in a model, an exponential moving average computed without no_grad. The second iteration's backward walks into the first iteration's freed graph. The fix is hidden = hidden.detach() at the start of each batch, which is exactly truncated backpropagation through time.

7. Turning recording off: no_grad, inference_mode, set_grad_enabled, detach

Recording costs time and memory, so you switch it off whenever you do not need gradients.

  • with torch.no_grad(): — operations are not recorded; outputs have requires_grad=False. Used for evaluation and for updates to parameters (optimisers do their in-place updates under no_grad, which is also why that is allowed on leaves).
  • with torch.inference_mode(): — like no_grad, plus tensors created inside skip version counting and view tracking. Outputs are inference tensors: on 2.14, c.is_inference() is True for them, and using one in a later autograd computation raises "Inference tensors cannot be saved for backward…", while modifying one in place outside the mode raises "Inplace update to inference tensor outside InferenceMode is not allowed". Use it for serving and evaluation; clone outputs if they must feed training.
  • torch.set_grad_enabled(flag) — a context manager or function that turns recording on or off by a boolean, handy for one loop that does both training and evaluation: with torch.set_grad_enabled(phase == "train"):.
  • t.detach() — not a mode but a per-tensor cut: returns a tensor that shares storage (and version counter) with t but has no grad_fn. Gradients do not flow through it. Used for targets computed from the model itself (a teacher's output in distillation, the stop-gradient in a target network), for carrying RNN state across batches, and before logging.

And remember the myth: model.eval() is none of these. It changes how dropout and BatchNorm behave (pt4); the graph is still recorded. An evaluation loop that calls model.eval() without no_grad or inference_mode keeps every activation of every batch alive until the outputs are dropped, and if those outputs are appended to a list, they never are.

8. Freezing parameters

To fine-tune only part of a model, set p.requires_grad_(False) on the parameters you want frozen. Autograd then computes no gradient for them — their .grad stays None, as you can check with a frozen nn.Linear weight while its bias still gets a gradient — and if no tensor upstream needs a gradient, it skips recording that part of the graph entirely, saving activation memory. Two traps: an optimiser built over model.parameters() still holds the frozen tensors (harmless for SGD and AdamW, which skip parameters with grad is None, but wasteful for optimiser state if they were ever unfrozen); and freezing by wrapping a submodule's forward in no_grad blocks gradients to everything before it as well, which is right for a frozen encoder at the start of the model and wrong for a frozen layer in the middle.

9. torch.autograd.grad and higher-order gradients

loss.backward() accumulates into leaves. torch.autograd.grad(outputs, inputs) instead returns the gradients with respect to the inputs you name, leaf or not, and touches no .grad. It is the functional way to ask for a gradient, used inside losses and in research code.

With create_graph=True, the backward computation is itself recorded, so the returned gradient has a grad_fn and can be differentiated again. For y = x³ at x = 2 (checked on 2.14): the first grad returns 12 (3x²) with a grad_fn, and a second grad of that returns 12 (6x). Uses include gradient penalties (a GAN discriminator penalised on the norm of its input gradient), Hessian–vector products for second-order analysis, and meta-learning. Cost: the backward pass's own intermediates are stored, so memory roughly doubles, and every operation on the path needs a differentiable backward.

10. Hooks

A hook is a function you register to be called during backward (or forward), with the power to observe or replace values.

  • t.register_hook(fn) — fn(grad) is called with the gradient flowing into tensor t; return a tensor to replace it. On 2.14, a hook returning g * 10 on a leaf makes its .grad ten times larger. Uses: per-tensor gradient clipping, gradient reversal layers, logging activation-gradient norms.
  • p.register_post_accumulate_grad_hook(fn) — fn(p) runs after p.grad has been accumulated for this backward. Its flagship use is fusing the optimiser step into backward: update p and set p.grad = None immediately, so gradients for the whole model never exist at once. The PyTorch tutorial on this technique reports large peak-memory savings for big models.
  • Module hooks — register_forward_hook, register_forward_pre_hook and register_full_backward_hook on an nn.Module see the module's inputs and outputs, or the gradients with respect to them. pt4 uses forward hooks to capture activations.

Every register_* returns a handle; call handle.remove() when done, or the hook stays forever — a quiet source of slowdowns and memory leaks in notebooks.

11. Writing your own autograd.Function

Sometimes you need a backward that is not the true derivative of the forward, or is cheaper or more stable than what autograd would derive. You subclass torch.autograd.Function. The current recommended style separates the forward from the context setup:

class RoundSTE(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(x):                      # no ctx: pure computation
        return x.round()

    @staticmethod
    def setup_context(ctx, inputs, output):
        pass                             # nothing to save for an STE

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_out):
        return grad_out                  # straight-through: pretend d(round)/dx = 1

y = RoundSTE.apply(x)                    # always call .apply, never forward()

Rules: backward returns one value per input of forward, with None for inputs that are not tensors or do not need gradients. Save tensors with ctx.save_for_backward(...) (which participates in the version check from pt1) and non-tensors as attributes on ctx. If forward modifies an input in place, declare it with ctx.mark_dirty. The older style — forward(ctx, x) doing both — still works.

Test every custom Function whose backward is meant to be exact with torch.autograd.gradcheck, which compares your backward with finite differences — in float64. On 2.14 a correct x² Function passes gradcheck in float64 and fails in float32 with "Jacobian mismatch", because finite differences in float32 lose too many digits; gradcheck also warns when inputs are not double precision. A straight-through estimator deliberately fails gradcheck, so test it by asserting that its backward returns the input gradient unchanged.

12. Python control flow, shared weights and non-differentiable points

Because the graph is recorded as the code runs, ordinary Python control flow just works. A loop that runs a layer a data-dependent number of times records that many nodes; an if on a Python value records only the branch taken; a recursive tree model records the tree it walked. Gradients flow only through the operations that actually ran this time. The flip side is that an if on a tensor value (if loss > 5:) needs that value on the CPU, which is a synchronisation on GPU (pt12), and the branch decision itself has no gradient — autograd differentiates the path taken, never the choice of path.

A parameter used in several places — a tied input embedding and output projection (pt4, pt10), a layer applied twice — appears once as a leaf with several outgoing edges. Backward sums the gradients arriving along every edge before the leaf's AccumulateGrad node runs, so the tied weight receives the total gradient of both uses. Nothing special is needed, which is why weight tying in PyTorch is one assignment.

Some operations have no useful gradient at all. Integer tensors cannot require gradients ("Only Tensors of floating point and complex dtype can require gradients"), so argmax, round, comparisons, indexing with computed indices and sampling from a categorical distribution all cut the gradient: the output of argmax has requires_grad=False. That is why discrete choices need tricks — the straight-through estimator, Gumbel-softmax relaxations, or policy-gradient estimators in reinforcement learning. At points where a function has a kink, PyTorch picks a convention, checked on 2.14: the derivative of relu at 0 is 0, of abs at 0 is 0, and when max() or amax() has ties the gradient is split evenly between the tied elements (each of two equal maxima gets 0.5), whereas max(dim=…) sends the whole gradient to the single index it returned. These conventions rarely matter for training, but they explain otherwise puzzling gradient values in tests.

13. NaN gradients from finite forwards

Some functions are finite where their derivatives are not. On 2.14:

q = torch.tensor([0.0], requires_grad=True)
(q.sqrt() * 0).sum().backward()
q.grad          # tensor([nan]): d sqrt/dq at 0 is inf, and 0 · inf = nan

The same happens with log(0), x / x.norm() at a zero vector, acos(±1) and pow(x, 0.5). A particularly sneaky version uses torch.where to "avoid" the bad region:

x = torch.tensor([-1.0, 4.0], requires_grad=True)
y = torch.where(x > 0, x.sqrt(), torch.zeros_like(x))   # forward is finite
y.sum().backward(); x.grad      # tensor([nan, 0.2500])

The forward never uses sqrt(-1), but backward computes the sqrt gradient for every element and then multiplies the unselected one by 0, and 0 · NaN is NaN. The fix is the "double where": make the dangerous input safe first, safe = torch.where(x > 0, x, torch.ones_like(x)), then apply the function to safe; the gradient becomes [0, 0.25]. Adding a small epsilon (sqrt(x + 1e-12), x / (x.norm() + eps)) is the other standard guard. To locate the first NaN in a large model, wrap the step in torch.autograd.detect_anomaly(): on 2.14 it raises "Function 'SqrtBackward0' returned nan values in its 0th output" and prints the forward line that created that node. It slows everything down noticeably, so use it only while debugging (pt9 builds the full NaN-hunting workflow).
deep:
How the engine schedules backward

The autograd engine is C++. When you call backward, it first walks the graph from the root to count, for every node, how many gradients will flow into it (its dependencies). It then runs a ready queue: a node becomes ready when all its incoming gradients have arrived and been summed. On CPU the work runs on the calling thread; for CUDA tensors there is a worker thread per device, and each backward op is queued on the same CUDA stream its forward ran on, so the backward pass is as asynchronous as the forward. Because nodes run as soon as they are ready, gradients for the last layers become available first — which is exactly what DDP exploits to start all-reducing gradient buckets while earlier layers are still computing (pt11).

Memory over time: why peak memory is at the start of backward

During the forward pass, saved tensors accumulate layer by layer, so memory climbs to its peak at the end of the forward and start of backward. As backward proceeds, each node releases its saved tensors after use while gradients for parameters are allocated. For a deep network the activation release dominates, and memory falls through the backward. This shape — a ramp up and a ramp down per step — is what you see in a memory timeline (pt7), and it is why activation checkpointing (saving fewer tensors in forward and recomputing them in backward) attacks the peak directly.

Saved-tensor hooks: deciding where activations live

torch.autograd.graph.saved_tensors_hooks(pack, unpack) lets you intercept every tensor autograd saves. pack is called at save time and can return anything — a CPU copy, a compressed form, a file handle; unpack turns it back into a tensor in backward. The built-in torch.autograd.graph.save_on_cpu(pin_memory=True) uses this to offload activations to host memory during forward and bring them back in backward, trading PCIe bandwidth for GPU memory. Activation checkpointing in its non-reentrant form (pt7) is also built on this mechanism: pack stores nothing but a recipe, and unpack recomputes.

The reentrant problem in custom Functions and checkpointing

A custom Function's backward runs inside the engine. If it calls autograd itself — running a forward under enable_grad and calling backward — that nested ("reentrant") backward runs as a separate graph traversal. The older reentrant implementation of activation checkpointing works this way and has real limitations: it does not support torch.autograd.grad, needs at least one input that requires grad, and recomputes the whole segment. That is why the docs recommend use_reentrant=False; on 2.14 calling checkpoint without the argument still only warns ("should be passed explicitly"), even though the warning text says that from 2.9 it would raise — pass it explicitly anyway.

Forward-mode AD and torch.func

Reverse mode computes v·J in one backward pass per output direction; forward mode computes J·u in one forward pass per input direction, carrying a tangent alongside each value. Forward mode wins when there are few inputs and many outputs — a Jacobian–vector product for sensitivity analysis, or one directional derivative. PyTorch supports it through torch.autograd.forward_ad and, more conveniently, torch.func.jvp. The torch.func module (formerly functorch) offers JAX-style composable transforms — grad, vjp, jvp, vmap, jacrev, hessian — over pure functions of parameters, which is the cleanest way to get per-example gradients (vmap(grad(f))) or Hessians. pt14 compares this style with JAX, where it is the only style.

Multiple losses, multiple backward calls, and partial graphs

When a model has several losses — a main loss and an auxiliary loss, or a generator and discriminator — the cheapest correct pattern is usually to sum them and call backward once: (loss_a + 0.1 * loss_b).backward() runs one traversal and frees the graph once. Calling backward on each loss separately needs retain_graph=True on all but the last, traverses the shared part twice, and keeps the shared saved tensors alive in between. torch.autograd.backward([loss_a, loss_b], [None, None]) runs several roots in one traversal. When different losses must update different parameter sets (as in a GAN), use torch.autograd.grad(loss, params_subset) or inputs= on backward to restrict which leaves receive gradients, and detach the tensors that cross the boundary so one loss does not push gradients into the other network.

When autograd's derivative is the wrong one

Autograd differentiates the code you wrote, not the mathematical function you meant. torch.norm(x) written as x.pow(2).sum().sqrt() has a NaN gradient at zero; a log-sum-exp written naively overflows in forward and backward; a softmax followed by log has a backward that underflows where log_softmax does not. Library functions such as F.cross_entropy, torch.logsumexp and F.normalize (which clamps the norm with an epsilon) exist precisely because their forward and backward were written for stability. Prefer them, and when you write a custom formula, consider a custom Function whose backward uses the stable analytic form — that is how FlashAttention-style kernels (gpu7) and fused cross-entropy implementations save both memory and accuracy.
prod:
Failure mode: evaluation runs out of memory

Symptom: training fits, but the evaluation loop OOMs or memory grows per batch. Cause: no no_grad/inference_mode, so every batch builds a graph; combined with appending outputs (or a loss tensor) to a list, every graph stays alive. Fix: wrap evaluation in torch.inference_mode(), call model.eval(), and log Python numbers (loss.item(), accepting the sync) or detached CPU tensors.

Failure mode: gradients that grow or are stale

Symptom: loss behaves as if the learning rate were rising, then diverges; or gradient norms grow linearly with steps. Cause: zero_grad missing or in the wrong place — after backward instead of before it, or once per epoch instead of per step. With gradient accumulation the bug is the opposite placement: zeroing inside the micro-batch loop throws away all but the last micro-batch. pt6 lays out the correct loop. A quick check: log the global gradient norm for the first few steps; it should not trend upward on a stable model.

Failure mode: "backward through the graph a second time"

Symptom: crash on the second iteration, typically in recurrent models, models with persistent state (memory tokens, running statistics you wrote yourself), or exponential-moving-average teachers. Cause: a tensor carried across iterations still holds last iteration's graph. Fix: detach() carried state at iteration boundaries; update EMA weights under no_grad. Resist the forum fix of retain_graph=True: it hides the bug and grows memory every step, because each iteration's graph now links to all previous ones.

Failure mode: frozen layers that move, trainable layers that don't

Symptom: a "frozen" backbone's weights change, or a newly added head never learns. Causes: freezing set after the optimiser captured parameter groups with weight decay (decoupled weight decay in AdamW only touches parameters with gradients, but momentum from earlier steps keeps moving them), a parameter re-created after the optimiser was built (the optimiser updates the old tensor), a tensor moved to the device after creation so it is not the leaf the optimiser holds, or a detach() left in the forward that cuts the head off from the loss. Diagnose by checking which parameters have non-None .grad after one backward, and by comparing parameter checksums before and after a step.

Failure mode: NaN gradients with finite loss

Symptom: loss is finite at step n, NaN at step n+1 because the update was NaN. Causes from the body: sqrt/log/norm at zero, where-masking an unsafe branch, division by a sum that can be zero (masked means over empty masks), and in mixed precision overflow in backward (pt7). Tools: detect_anomaly to locate the op; a hook on each parameter that asserts torch.isfinite(grad).all() to locate the layer; and clip_grad_norm_(..., error_if_nonfinite=True) to stop on the first bad step rather than training on garbage.

Observability

Teams that train large models log the global gradient norm every step (the value clip_grad_norm_ returns), per-layer gradient norms periodically, and the fraction of steps where clipping engaged. A gradient-norm spike that precedes a loss spike is the standard early warning in large-model training, discussed in pt9. These metrics are nearly free: the norm is computed anyway if you clip.
myths: loss.backward() computes the gradient and stores it, replacing the old one.

It adds into each leaf's .grad. Call backward three times without zeroing and .grad holds the sum of three gradients. This is deliberate — it makes gradient accumulation across micro-batches trivial — and it is why every training loop needs zero_grad() in the right place (pt6).
model.eval() turns off gradient tracking.

eval() only switches modules such as dropout and BatchNorm to inference behaviour (pt4). The graph is still recorded and activations are still saved unless you also use torch.no_grad() or torch.inference_mode(). Forgetting this is a classic evaluation-loop memory blow-up.
torch.no_grad() and torch.inference_mode() are the same thing.

Both stop graph recording. inference_mode also skips version counting and view tracking, so it is slightly faster, but the tensors it creates are 'inference tensors' that can never be used in a later autograd computation or modified in place outside the mode. Use inference_mode for pure serving and evaluation, no_grad for updates and for anything whose results may feed training.
detach() copies the tensor.

detach() returns a view that shares storage and the version counter with the original but has no grad_fn. Modifying the detached tensor in place changes the original and can still trigger the in-place check. Use detach().clone() when you need an independent copy.
If a gradient is NaN, the forward pass must have produced a NaN.

The forward can be perfectly finite while the backward is not. sqrt(0) has an infinite derivative, so (x.sqrt() * 0) at x = 0 gives a forward value of 0 and a gradient of 0 × ∞ = NaN. torch.where does not save you: the gradient of the unselected branch is multiplied by zero, and 0 × NaN is still NaN.
Non-leaf tensors have a .grad you can inspect after backward.

Only leaves get .grad populated. For an intermediate tensor, .grad is None and PyTorch warns. Call .retain_grad() on it before backward, or register a hook, or use torch.autograd.grad to get the gradient directly.
lab:
CPU, PyTorch 2.14 in gpt_env; about 15 minutes. Save as pt3_lab.py.

import torch
# 1. trace the graph and check the hand computation
x, w, b = (torch.tensor(v, requires_grad=True) for v in (2.0, 3.0, 1.0))
L = (w * x + b).relu() ** 2
node, depth = L.grad_fn, 0
while node is not None:
    print("  " * depth, type(node).__name__)
    node = node.next_functions[0][0] if node.next_functions else None; depth += 1
L.backward(); print("grads w x b:", w.grad.item(), x.grad.item(), b.grad.item())

# 2. accumulation and the second-backward error
L2 = (w * x) ** 2
L2.backward(retain_graph=True); L2.backward()
print("w.grad after two backward:", w.grad.item())   # 28 + 24 + 24
try:
    L2.backward()
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("third:", str(e)[:50])

# 3. no_grad vs inference_mode
with torch.no_grad(): a = w * 2
with torch.inference_mode(): c = w * 2
print("no_grad inference?", a.is_inference(), " inference_mode?", c.is_inference())
try:
    (c * w).backward()
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("inference tensor:", str(e)[:45])

# 4. the where-NaN trap and its fix
z = torch.tensor([-1.0, 4.0], requires_grad=True)
torch.where(z > 0, z.sqrt(), 0.0).sum().backward(); print("naive:", z.grad)
z.grad = None
s = torch.where(z > 0, z, 1.0)
torch.where(z > 0, s.sqrt(), 0.0).sum().backward(); print("safe:", z.grad)

# 5. a custom Function checked with gradcheck
class Cube(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, t): ctx.save_for_backward(t); return t ** 3
    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, g): (t,) = ctx.saved_tensors; return 3 * t ** 2 * g
t64 = torch.randn(5, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
print("gradcheck:", torch.autograd.gradcheck(Cube.apply, (t64,)))
  1. Step 1 prints the chain PowBackward0 → ReluBackward0 → AddBackward0 → MulBackward0 → AccumulateGrad, and grads 28, 42, 14 — matching the body's trace.
  2. Step 2: w.grad accumulates (the 28 from step 1 plus two more backward passes of 2·(w·x)·x = 24); the third backward fails because the second freed the graph.
  3. Step 3: only the inference-mode tensor reports is_inference() == True, and it is rejected by autograd.
  4. Step 4: naive gives [nan, 0.25]; safe gives [0, 0.25].
  5. Step 5 prints True. Break the backward (return 2 * t * g) and watch gradcheck fail; switch to float32 and watch even the correct version fail.
recap: Autograd records a graph while the forward pass runs: every operation on a tensor that requires grad creates a node (grad_fn) linked to the nodes of its inputs, and saves whatever its backward formula needs.
Leaf tensors are created by you (parameters, inputs); non-leaf tensors are results of operations. backward() fills .grad only on leaves that require grad, and it adds to whatever is already there.

backward() walks the graph from the output in reverse order, multiplying vectors by local Jacobians (vector–Jacobian products), and frees saved tensors as it goes; a second backward needs retain_graph=True.
A non-scalar output needs an explicit gradient argument, because backward computes v·J for a chosen v, not the full Jacobian.

torch.no_grad() stops recording; torch.inference_mode() also skips version and view bookkeeping and produces tensors that cannot re-enter autograd; detach() cuts one tensor out of the graph without copying.
Hooks let you observe or rewrite gradients: tensor.register_hook for a tensor's gradient, register_post_accumulate_grad_hook after a parameter's .grad is updated, and module backward hooks.
torch.autograd.grad returns gradients instead of accumulating them, and create_graph=True makes the gradient itself differentiable for second-order methods and gradient penalties.

A custom torch.autograd.Function supplies forward and backward by hand — for straight-through estimators, numerically stable formulas, or memory savings — and must be verified with gradcheck in float64.
NaN gradients often come from the backward of a finite forward (sqrt or log at 0, division by a tiny norm); torch.where needs a 'safe' input in the unused branch to avoid them.
glossary: A debug mode (torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly or detect_anomaly) that records forward stack traces and raises when a backward function returns NaN.
PyTorch's automatic differentiation engine, which records operations on tensors and computes gradients by reverse-mode differentiation.
Backpropagating through the unrolled steps of a recurrent model; truncated BPTT cuts the graph every few steps by detaching the hidden state.
An argument to backward/grad that records the backward computation itself, so the resulting gradients can be differentiated again.
Return a tensor that shares data with the original but has no autograd history; gradients do not flow through it.
A computation graph built anew on every forward pass as the Python code runs, so control flow can differ between iterations (also called define-by-run).
A running average updated as avg = d·avg + (1−d)·new, used for teacher networks and averaged weights; update it under no_grad.
The node in the autograd graph that produced a tensor, which knows how to compute gradients for that operation's inputs.
A utility that compares analytical gradients with finite-difference estimates; reliable only in float64.
A function you register to be called with a gradient (or a module's inputs or outputs) during forward or backward, able to inspect or replace it.
torch.inference_mode(): a context that disables autograd and its bookkeeping; tensors made inside it cannot later be used in autograd.
The matrix of partial derivatives of every output with respect to every input of a function.
A tensor not produced by a recorded operation: parameters and user-created inputs. Gradients accumulate into its .grad.
torch.no_grad(): a context in which operations are not recorded, so results have requires_grad=False.
A flag on a tensor saying that autograd should track operations on it; results of operations inherit it if any input has it.
An argument to backward that keeps the saved tensors so the same graph can be backpropagated again.
Automatic differentiation that computes gradients from the output back to the inputs; one pass gives the gradient of a scalar with respect to all inputs.
A tensor kept by a graph node during the forward pass because its backward formula needs it; it lives until backward frees it.
A custom backward that passes the gradient through a non-differentiable operation (rounding, clamping) as if it were the identity.
The product of an upstream gradient vector with a function's Jacobian, which is what each backward node computes without forming the Jacobian.
drill:
Find the bug: an RNN language model that crashes, then leaks, then stops learning

This truncated-BPTT loop trains a small LSTM language model. Version 1 crashed on the second batch with "Trying to backward through the graph a second time". Someone "fixed" it. Now memory grows every batch and, after a few hundred steps, loss stops improving even though the learning rate is fine. Find every bug.

hidden = model.init_hidden(batch_size)
for x, y in loader:
    out, hidden = model(x, hidden)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(out.view(-1, V), y.view(-1))
    loss.backward(retain_graph=True)      # the "fix"
    optimizer.step()
    history.append(loss)
    if step % 100 == 0:
        model.eval()
        val = evaluate(model)             # evaluate() runs the val loader and returns a float
    optimizer.zero_grad()
Answer

Bug 1 — hidden state carries the graph across batches. hidden returned by this batch is the input to the next, so batch 2's graph links back into batch 1's. The original crash was backward walking into batch 1's freed graph. retain_graph=True stopped the crash by keeping every batch's graph alive, so each backward now traverses the entire history (slower every step) and memory grows without bound. Fix: hidden = tuple(h.detach() for h in hidden) at the start of each iteration (truncated BPTT), and remove retain_graph=True.

Bug 2 — the history list keeps graphs alive. history.append(loss) stores the loss tensor with its grad_fn, which references every saved activation of that step. Even after fixing bug 1, memory grows by one step's activations per iteration. Fix: history.append(loss.item()) (a sync per step; acceptable here, or log every N steps) or loss.detach().

Bug 3 — eval() is never undone. After the first evaluation the model stays in eval mode, so dropout is off for the rest of training; if the model had BatchNorm it would also stop updating its statistics. Symptom: training loss improves faster for a while (no dropout noise) and validation stalls, read as "stops learning". Fix: call model.train() after evaluate, and make evaluate itself run under torch.inference_mode() and restore the previous mode.

Not a bug, but worth saying: zero_grad() at the end of the loop is fine — it runs before the next backward. The common form puts it first; both are correct as long as exactly one zero_grad happens between consecutive steps.

Find the bug: the cosine-similarity loss that produces NaN on step 1

A contrastive loss computes sim = (a * b).sum(-1) / (a.pow(2).sum(-1).sqrt() * b.pow(2).sum(-1).sqrt()). Some rows of a are all zeros (padding embeddings). The loss is finite, but the first update makes every parameter NaN. Why, and what is the minimal fix?

Answer

For a zero row the norm is sqrt(0), whose derivative is infinite; the forward also divides 0 by 0, giving NaN similarity for that row — if the row is then masked out of the loss with a multiplication by 0 or a where, the forward loss becomes finite again but backward still computes the gradient through the NaN and the infinite sqrt derivative, and 0 · NaN = NaN reaches every parameter that fed a. Minimal fix: use F.cosine_similarity(a, b, dim=-1, eps=1e-8) or F.normalize, which clamp the norm away from zero, and drop padding rows before computing the similarity rather than masking afterwards. Confirm with detect_anomaly, which will name SqrtBackward0 or DivBackward0.
qa: E
What is a leaf tensor, and which tensors get .grad populated?

A leaf is a tensor that was not produced by a recorded operation — parameters and inputs you created yourself. After backward, .grad is populated only on leaves with requires_grad=True. Intermediate tensors have grad_fn set and .grad None unless you call retain_grad() on them.
E
Why do training loops call optimizer.zero_grad()?

Because backward() adds into .grad rather than overwriting it. Without zeroing, each step's gradient includes every previous step's, so updates grow and point in stale directions. Since PyTorch 2.0 zero_grad sets .grad to None by default (set_to_none=True), which saves a memset and lets the next backward allocate fresh gradients.
Follow-up: When is accumulation what you want? — Gradient accumulation: call backward on several micro-batches, each scaled by 1/k, then step once, to simulate a k-times-larger batch.
E
What is the difference between model.eval() and torch.no_grad()?

eval() changes module behaviour — dropout off, BatchNorm uses running statistics. no_grad() stops autograd from recording, so no graph and no saved activations. An evaluation loop needs both: eval() for correct outputs, no_grad() or inference_mode() for memory and speed.
M
Walk through what happens during loss.backward() for y = w·x + b, z = relu(y), L = z² with x = 2, w = 3, b = 1.

Forward: y = 7, z = 7, L = 49; the graph is PowBackward → ReluBackward → AddBackward → MulBackward, with leaves w, x, b. Backward starts with dL/dL = 1. PowBackward gives dL/dz = 2z = 14. ReluBackward passes 14 because y > 0. AddBackward sends 14 to both w·x and b, so b.grad = 14. MulBackward multiplies by the other factor: w.grad = 14·2 = 28, x.grad = 14·3 = 42. Each node frees its saved tensors once used.
Follow-up: What did each node save? — PowBackward saved z, ReluBackward saved its output (to know where y > 0), MulBackward saved w and x; AddBackward saved nothing.
M
What does 'Trying to backward through the graph a second time' mean and how do you fix it?

backward frees the saved tensors of the graph as it goes to release memory, so a second backward over the same graph has nothing to work with. If you genuinely need two backward passes through shared parts (two losses on one forward, or some meta-learning setups), pass retain_graph=True to the first. More often the bug is a tensor carried across iterations that still references last step's graph — for example a hidden state in an RNN not detached between batches — and the fix is detach().

Follow-up: Why is retain_graph=True everywhere a bad fix? — It keeps every activation alive until the graph is garbage-collected, multiplying memory, and hides the real bug of a graph spanning iterations.
M
Compare torch.no_grad() and torch.inference_mode().

Both disable recording, so outputs do not require grad. inference_mode additionally disables version counter bumps and view tracking for tensors created inside, which removes a little overhead per op. The cost is that those 'inference tensors' cannot be saved for backward later ('Inference tensors cannot be saved for backward') or updated in place outside the mode. Use inference_mode for serving and evaluation; use no_grad for parameter updates, EMA weights and anything whose outputs may enter training.
Follow-up: How do you use an inference tensor in training anyway? — Clone it outside inference mode; the clone is a normal tensor.
M
Why does backward() on a non-scalar output raise 'grad can be implicitly created only for scalar outputs'?

Reverse mode computes a vector–Jacobian product v·J, not the Jacobian itself. For a scalar output v is just 1, so PyTorch supplies it. For a vector output you must choose v — pass gradient=torch.ones_like(out) to get the gradient of out.sum(), or reduce to a scalar loss first. Computing a full Jacobian needs one backward per output (or torch.func.jacrev with vmap).
Follow-up: When is forward mode cheaper? — When there are few inputs and many outputs: forward mode costs one pass per input direction, reverse mode one per output.
M
How do you freeze part of a model, and what happens to its gradients?

Set requires_grad_(False) on the parameters to freeze. Autograd then does not compute gradients for them — their .grad stays None — and if nothing upstream needs gradients, it does not even save activations for that part. Also pass only trainable parameters to the optimiser, or at least make sure weight decay does not move frozen weights (AdamW skips parameters whose .grad is None).
M
Your loss is finite but some gradients are NaN. Name two causes and how to find them.

Backward formulas with infinities at points where the forward is finite: sqrt at 0 (derivative 1/(2·√0)), log at 0, x/‖x‖ when the norm is 0, acos at ±1. And torch.where over an unsafe branch: the unselected branch's gradient is multiplied by 0, but 0·NaN = NaN. Find them with torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True), which raises at the first backward function returning NaN and prints the forward line that created it, or with tensor hooks that check torch.isfinite on each gradient.
Follow-up: How do you fix the where case? — Make the unused branch's input safe: s = torch.where(x > 0, x, 1.0); y = torch.where(x > 0, s.sqrt(), 0.0).
H
Write a custom autograd.Function for a straight-through estimator of rounding, and explain how you would test it.

forward returns x.round(); backward returns the incoming gradient unchanged, as if rounding were the identity. In the modern style forward(x) is a staticmethod without ctx, setup_context(ctx, inputs, output) saves what backward needs, and backward(ctx, grad) returns one gradient per forward input (None for non-tensors). Test it by checking the backward returns grad unchanged; gradcheck is not appropriate here because the STE deliberately differs from the true derivative (zero almost everywhere). For a Function that is meant to be exact, use gradcheck in float64.
Follow-up: Why float64 for gradcheck? — Finite differences with a small epsilon lose most of float32's 7 digits to cancellation; the check then reports mismatches for correct code.
H
What are gradient hooks used for in practice, and which hook would you use for each?

tensor.register_hook(fn) receives the gradient flowing into a tensor and may return a replacement: gradient clipping or scaling per tensor, logging gradient norms of activations, or gradient reversal. Tensor.register_post_accumulate_grad_hook(fn) runs after a parameter's .grad has been accumulated, which is how optimiser-in-backward works: update and free each parameter's gradient immediately to cut peak memory. Module full backward hooks see gradients with respect to a module's inputs and outputs. DDP itself uses autograd hooks to start all-reduces as soon as a bucket of gradients is ready (pt11).
H
Explain create_graph=True and give a use case.

Normally the backward pass is not itself recorded. With create_graph=True, the operations of the backward pass are recorded, so the gradients are tensors with their own grad_fn and can be differentiated again. Uses: a gradient penalty (WGAN-GP penalises ‖∇ₓD(x)‖ − 1, so the loss contains a gradient), second-order optimisation and Hessian–vector products, and meta-learning such as MAML. Cost: the graph of the backward pass must be stored, roughly doubling memory, and second derivatives must exist for every op (custom Functions need a differentiable backward).
Follow-up: How do you get a Hessian–vector product cheaply? — g = grad(L, w, create_graph=True); hv = grad(g @ v, w): two backward passes, never forming the Hessian.
H
Why did PyTorch choose a dynamic (define-by-run) graph, and what does it cost?

Recording the graph as ordinary Python executes means any control flow — loops of data-dependent length, recursion, if statements on values — just works, and debugging uses normal Python tools. The PyTorch paper (NeurIPS 2019) gives the reason: Python is too dynamic for ahead-of-time source-to-source differentiation, so PyTorch overloads operators and rebuilds the representation of the function every time it runs. The cost is per-op Python and bookkeeping overhead and no whole-program view for optimisation, which is what torch.compile adds back by capturing graphs from the same code (pt12).

Follow-up: How does the dynamic graph free memory early? — Each node holds only references to its saved tensors and the next nodes; as backward runs, nodes release their saved tensors, so peak memory falls during backward instead of at the end.

t: nn.Module: parameters, buffers, state_dict, train/eval, hooks and initialisation
sum: What nn.Module actually does: registration of parameters, buffers and submodules, the state_dict and loading pitfalls, what train() and eval() change, forward and backward hooks, default and GPT-style initialisation, weight tying, and counting parameters correctly.
prereq: pt3
Autograd records operations on tensors that require grad; leaves get .grad; no_grad and inference_mode stop recording; hooks can observe or replace gradients.
dl4
BatchNorm normalises each channel with batch statistics in training and running averages at inference; LayerNorm and RMSNorm normalise each example's features and behave the same in both modes.
dl8
Dropout zeroes activations at random with probability p during training and scales the survivors by 1/(1−p), so nothing needs rescaling at inference.
mc15
The NumPy BatchNorm keeps running mean and variance updated with momentum, and uses them instead of batch statistics at test time.
why:
A team adds a stack of adapter layers to a pretrained model. They write self.adapters = [Adapter(d) for _ in range(n_layers)], train for a day, and evaluation looks exactly like the base model. It is exactly the base model: the adapters lived in a Python list, so model.parameters() never returned them, the optimiser never touched them, and the checkpoint did not even contain them. Another team fine-tunes a vision model with batch size 2 per GPU and watches validation accuracy collapse, because BatchNorm in training mode computes statistics from two images. A third loads a checkpoint with strict=False "because of some prefix issue" and ships a model in which every attention layer silently kept its random initial weights.

All three are failures of the same piece of machinery: nn.Module. It looks like a thin base class — you subclass it, assign layers in __init__, write forward — but it does a lot behind the scenes. It registers parameters, buffers and submodules so that optimisers, device moves, checkpoints and mode switches can find them. It names every tensor with a dotted path that becomes the key in a saved file. It carries a training flag that changes what dropout and normalisation layers compute. It lets you attach hooks that see inputs, outputs and gradients. And its default initialisation is a specific formula that transformer code almost always replaces.

ML-debugging interviews lean on this because the bugs are realistic and silent: the model runs, the loss even goes down, and the problem is invisible unless you know what registration, state dicts and modes do. "Which of these layers will be trained?", "why is this checkpoint loading half the model?", "why is the eval loss different from what you get on the training data in eval mode?", "count the parameters of this model" — each has a precise answer.

This lesson covers how registration works and its pitfalls (plain tensors, Python lists, ModuleDict rules), parameters versus buffers, state_dict and the load-time mismatches you will meet, exactly what train() and eval() change (with BatchNorm traced by hand), forward and backward hooks, default and GPT-style initialisation and how to check it, weight tying, and counting parameters correctly — using GPT-2 small, worked through to the last parameter, and nanoGPT's model file as the real code to compare with.
primer:
Think of an nn.Module as a filing cabinet with three labelled drawers and a switch on the front. Whenever you assign something in __init__, the cabinet looks at it and decides which drawer it belongs in:

  • an nn.Parameter — a tensor you want trained — goes into the parameters drawer;
  • another nn.Module — a layer, a block — goes into the submodules drawer, and is itself a cabinet with its own drawers;
  • a tensor you register with register_buffer — state that is not trained, such as BatchNorm's running averages or a causal mask — goes into the buffers drawer.

Anything else — a plain tensor, a Python list of layers, a number — is left on top of the cabinet. Every whole-model operation opens the drawers, recursively, and ignores what is on top: parameters() collects the parameters drawer of every cabinet for the optimiser; .to("cuda") moves parameters and buffers; state_dict() writes out parameters and buffers under their drawer paths (blocks.3.attn.proj.weight); train() and eval() flip the switch on every cabinet.

The switch is the training flag, self.training. Layers that behave differently while learning read it: dropout drops only when it is True; BatchNorm uses the current batch's statistics and updates its running averages only when it is True. It has nothing to do with gradients — that is autograd's recorder from pt3, switched with no_grad.

Here is a small module and what each line does to the cabinet:

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, C):
        super().__init__()                       # creates the three empty drawers
        self.up = nn.Linear(C, 4 * C)             # submodule "up" (with its own up.weight, up.bias)
        self.down = nn.Linear(4 * C, C)           # submodule "down"
        self.gain = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(C))   # parameter "gain"
        self.register_buffer("calls", torch.zeros((), dtype=torch.long))  # buffer "calls"
        self.note = "relu MLP"                    # plain attribute: ignored
    def forward(self, x):                         # x: (B, T, C)
        self.calls += 1                           # buffers can be updated in forward
        return self.down(self.up(x).relu()) * self.gain

list(MLP(8).state_dict()) is ['gain', 'calls', 'up.weight', 'up.bias', 'down.weight', 'down.bias'] — the module's own parameters and buffers first, then each submodule's under its prefix. MLP(8).to("cuda") moves all six tensors. MLP(8).parameters() yields five tensors (not calls). MLP(8).eval() flips training on the MLP and on up and down. And note is just a Python attribute — fine for configuration strings, wrong for tensors.

Where the analogy breaks: a filing cabinet does not care where the same document is filed twice, but a module can hold one Parameter in two drawers — that is weight tying — and then parameters() de-duplicates it while state_dict() lists it under both paths. And unlike a cabinet, a module has behaviour: its forward method, which you call by calling the module itself (model(x), never model.forward(x), because calling the module also runs any hooks).

If you remember one sentence: nn.Module only knows about Parameters, buffers and submodules you registered; every optimiser, device move, checkpoint and mode switch works through that registry, and the training flag changes layer behaviour, not gradient recording.
body:
1. How registration works

nn.Module overrides Python's attribute assignment (__setattr__). When you write self.proj = nn.Linear(768, 768), it sees a Module and stores it in an internal ordered dictionary, self._modules["proj"]. self.gain = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(768)) goes into self._parameters["gain"]. self.register_buffer("mask", torch.tril(torch.ones(T, T))) goes into self._buffers["mask"]. Everything else goes into the ordinary instance dictionary. You must call super().__init__() before assigning any of these, or the internal dictionaries do not exist yet and the assignment raises.

Every recursive operation walks those three dictionaries and builds dotted names from the path: a parameter weight inside proj inside the third element of blocks is blocks.2.proj.weight. Those names are what named_parameters() yields, what keys the state_dict, and what optimiser parameter groups and FSDP wrapping policies (pt11) match on.

A run on 2.14 with a module that has a registered Linear, a Python list of two Linears, a plain tensor attribute, two buffers (one non-persistent) and a BatchNorm:

named_parameters: ['lin.weight', 'lin.bias', 'bn.weight', 'bn.bias']
named_buffers:    ['mask', 'cache', 'bn.running_mean', 'bn.running_var',
                   'bn.num_batches_tracked']
state_dict keys:  ['mask', 'lin.weight', 'lin.bias', 'bn.weight', 'bn.bias',
                   'bn.running_mean', 'bn.running_var', 'bn.num_batches_tracked']

The two Linears in the list and the plain scale tensor appear nowhere. The non-persistent buffer cache is a buffer (it moves with .to()) but is not in the state_dict.

2. Containers: ModuleList, ModuleDict, Sequential

To hold a variable number of layers, use a container that registers its contents:

  • nn.ModuleList([...]) registers each element under its index (blocks.0, blocks.1, …). It has no forward; you loop over it yourself, which is what transformers do.
  • nn.ModuleDict({...}) registers each value under its key. Keys must be strings and cannot contain a dot (on 2.14: "module name can't contain \".\", got: a.b"), because dots are the path separator. Iteration order is insertion order.
  • nn.Sequential(...) registers its elements and has a forward that applies them in order — good for simple stacks, awkward when a layer needs more than one input.
  • nn.ParameterList and nn.ParameterDict do the same for bare Parameters.

Pitfalls beyond the plain-list bug: replacing a ModuleList element in place (self.blocks[3] = NewBlock()) works, but an optimiser built earlier still holds the old block's parameters; and building the list inside forward creates new, unregistered, randomly initialised layers on every call.

3. Parameters versus buffers

A parameter is an nn.Parameter, a tensor subclass with requires_grad=True by default; model.parameters() hands it to the optimiser. A buffer is model state that must travel with the model but is not trained by gradient descent:

  • BatchNorm's running_mean, running_var and num_batches_tracked — updated by the layer itself in training mode.
  • A precomputed causal mask, as in nanoGPT's non-flash attention path (self.register_buffer("bias", torch.tril(...))).
  • Rotary-embedding frequency tables or cached sin/cos values — usually persistent=False, since they can be recomputed and should not bloat or constrain checkpoints.
  • Exponential-moving-average statistics, quantisation scales, vocab masks.

Why not just use a Parameter with requires_grad=False? Because the optimiser would still hold it, weight decay code that iterates over parameter groups might touch it, and parameter counts would include it. Buffers say "state, not weights".

4. state_dict, and loading it safely

model.state_dict() returns an ordered dictionary from dotted names to tensors (parameters and persistent buffers), detached from autograd. It is the unit of saving: torch.save(model.state_dict(), path) rather than pickling the whole model object, so the file contains tensors and names, not your class definitions (pt8 covers why that matters for security and refactoring).

model.load_state_dict(sd, strict=True) copies values into existing tensors by name. With the default strict=True, any mismatch raises, as on 2.14:

Error(s) in loading state_dict for M:
    Missing key(s) in state_dict: "lin.bias".
    Unexpected key(s) in state_dict: "extra.weight".

With strict=False it loads what matches and returns _IncompatibleKeys(missing_keys=['lin.bias'], unexpected_keys=['extra.weight']). Shape mismatches raise either way. Rules that prevent most loading bugs:

  • Prefixes. DistributedDataParallel and DataParallel wrap your model as .module, so a state_dict saved from the wrapper has keys like module.encoder.weight. torch.compile returns a wrapper whose state_dict keys start with _orig_mod.. Save the unwrapped model's state_dict, or strip the prefix with a dictionary comprehension at load time.
  • Never ignore the return value of strict=False. Assert that missing_keys contains only what you expect (a new head) and log unexpected_keys.
  • Dtype and device. load_state_dict copies into the model's existing tensors, converting dtype and device to match them. To load onto the meta device or adopt the checkpoint's tensors directly, use assign=True (pt8).

5. train() and eval(): exactly what changes

model.train() sets self.training = True on the model and all submodules; model.eval() is model.train(False). On 2.14, after m.eval(), m.training, m.bn.training and m.lin.training are all False. The modules that care:

Dropout in training mode zeroes each element with probability p and multiplies survivors by 1/(1−p) — with p = 0.5, a vector of ones becomes something like [0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0]. In eval mode it returns its input unchanged. Because of the scaling during training, no rescaling is needed at inference ("inverted dropout", dl8).

BatchNorm in training mode normalises each channel with the current batch's mean and (biased) variance, and updates its running statistics: running = (1 − momentum) · running + momentum · batch_statistic, with momentum 0.1 by default and the unbiased batch variance used for the running estimate. A hand-checked trace on 2.14 with a fresh BatchNorm1d(2) (running mean 0, running variance 1) and the batch [[1, 10], [3, 30]]:

ChannelBatch meanUnbiased batch varianceNew running meanNew running variance
0220.9·0 + 0.1·2 = 0.20.9·1 + 0.1·2 = 1.1
1202000.9·0 + 0.1·20 = 2.00.9·1 + 0.1·200 = 20.9

In eval mode BatchNorm uses those running values and does not update them. That is why the same input gives different outputs in the two modes, why evaluating in training mode quietly corrupts the running statistics with evaluation data, and why tiny batches are a problem: statistics from two samples are noise, and with one sample per channel training mode refuses outright ("Expected more than 1 value per channel when training"). LayerNorm and RMSNorm normalise each example on its own and behave identically in both modes, which is one reason transformers use them.

Other modules check the flag too. nn.MultiheadAttention uses an inference fast path only when not training; F.scaled_dot_product_attention, being a function, does not know the mode, so its dropout_p must be set to 0 in eval by the calling module — the docs show dropout_p=(self.p if self.training else 0.0), and forgetting it is a planted bug in pt10. Any custom module can branch on self.training.

6. Modules versus torch.nn.functional

Almost every layer has a stateless functional twin in torch.nn.functional (imported as F): nn.Linear and F.linear, nn.Dropout and F.dropout, nn.LayerNorm and F.layer_norm, nn.CrossEntropyLoss and F.cross_entropy. The module version owns its parameters and knows the training flag; the functional version takes everything as arguments. The rule: if it has learnable weights or mode-dependent behaviour, use the module so registration and train/eval work; if it is a pure function of its inputs (F.relu, F.softmax, F.cross_entropy), the functional form is simpler.

The trap sits exactly on that boundary. F.dropout(x, p=0.1) has a training argument that defaults to True — it does not read any module's flag — so a model that calls F.dropout(x, 0.1) in its forward keeps dropping out during evaluation. Write F.dropout(x, 0.1, training=self.training) or use an nn.Dropout submodule. F.scaled_dot_product_attention's dropout_p has the same property, as noted above. Likewise F.batch_norm needs you to pass the running statistics and the training flag yourself. When reviewing code for a debugging round, every functional call with a mode-dependent behaviour is a place to look.

7. Walking a model: modules, children, apply

Four methods let you visit the tree. children() yields direct submodules; modules() and named_modules() yield every module recursively, starting with the model itself, with dotted names; apply(fn) calls fn on every submodule (children first, then the parent) and is the standard way to run an init function. Typical uses: count layers of a type (sum(isinstance(m, nn.Linear) for m in model.modules())), swap all nn.GELU for another activation by assigning to the parent's attribute, freeze every normalisation layer, or attach a forward hook to each block. Swapping must be done on the parent (setattr(parent, name, new)), since assigning to the loop variable changes nothing. print(model) shows the registered tree — another quick registration check: a layer that does not appear in the printout is not registered.

8. Moving and casting modules

model.to(device), .cuda(), .half(), .bfloat16() and .to(dtype) on a module modify its parameters and buffers in place and return the module itself (on 2.14, m.to(torch.float64) is m is True) — unlike tensor.to, which returns a new tensor. Two consequences: build the optimiser after moving the model (on older versions moving could replace parameter tensors; today the parameter objects are kept, but the habit costs nothing), and casting a module to float16 also casts BatchNorm's running statistics and every buffer, which is often not what you want — mixed precision (pt7) keeps weights in float32 and casts per operation instead.

Tensors created inside forward must follow the input: torch.arange(T, device=x.device), torch.zeros_like(x), x.new_zeros(shape). A bare torch.arange(T) works on CPU and fails on GPU with "Expected all tensors to be on the same device".

9. Hooks on modules

Modules accept three kinds of hook (pt3 covered tensor-level hooks):

  • register_forward_pre_hook(fn) — fn(module, args) runs before forward and may return modified inputs.
  • register_forward_hook(fn) — fn(module, args, output) runs after forward and may return a replacement output.
  • register_full_backward_hook(fn) — fn(module, grad_input, grad_output) runs when gradients with respect to the module's inputs have been computed.

Hooks let you instrument a model you do not want to edit: capture activations for analysis or distillation, record per-layer activation statistics to check initialisation, log output shapes to debug a shape error (pt2's method), or add a steering vector to a layer's output. Each call returns a RemovableHandle; keep it and call .remove() when done. Store output.detach(), not output, or the hook keeps the graph alive. Hooks run only when you call the module (model(x)); calling model.forward(x) directly skips them.

10. Initialisation: the defaults and what transformers use

PyTorch initialises layers in their constructor via reset_parameters(). For nn.Linear on 2.14 the code is init.kaiming_uniform_(self.weight, a=math.sqrt(5)), with a comment noting this equals U(−1/√in_features, 1/√in_features); the bias uses the same bound. For a 768-input layer the bound is 1/√768 ≈ 0.0361, and the standard deviation of a uniform distribution on ±b is b/√3 ≈ 0.0208 (measured: 0.0208). Convolutions use the same rule with fan_in = in_channels × kernel area. nn.Embedding uses N(0, 1) — standard deviation 1 (measured: 0.99), about fifty times larger than a typical transformer weight. Normalisation layers start with weight 1 and bias 0.

GPT-2-style models replace these. nanoGPT's _init_weights, applied with self.apply(...), sets every Linear weight and every Embedding to N(0, 0.02) and biases to zero, then walks named_parameters() and re-initialises every parameter whose name ends in c_proj.weight — the projections that write into the residual stream — with standard deviation 0.02/√(2·n_layer), "per GPT-2 paper". The reasoning: the residual stream is a sum of 2·n_layer contributions (attention and MLP in each block); if each has variance σ², the sum has variance 2·n_layer·σ², so scaling σ by 1/√(2·n_layer) keeps the stream's scale independent of depth.

The quickest check that an initialisation is sane is the loss at step 0. For a V-way softmax with small logits, the predicted distribution is close to uniform and the cross-entropy is ln V: ln 50,257 ≈ 10.82 for GPT-2's vocabulary, ln 10 ≈ 2.30 for a 10-class classifier. Karpathy's Recipe calls this "verify loss @ init". A step-0 loss well above ln V means the logits are too large — confident random guesses — and the first hundred steps are spent undoing the initialisation.

11. Weight tying

A language model maps token ids to vectors with an embedding matrix of shape (V, C) and maps final hidden states back to vocabulary logits with an output projection nn.Linear(C, V, bias=False), whose weight is also (V, C). Weight tying makes them the same tensor. In nanoGPT it is one line:

self.transformer.wte.weight = self.lm_head.weight   # assign the same Parameter

Both modules now refer to one Parameter. In the forward pass it is used twice; in backward, autograd sums the two gradient contributions before accumulating into its .grad (pt3). It saves V × C parameters — 38.6M for GPT-2 small — and, empirically, tends to help small and medium language models. Bookkeeping consequences, checked on 2.14: g.head.weight is g.wte.weight is True; parameters() yields the tensor once; state_dict() contains both wte.weight and head.weight, pointing at the same storage. Tying must be re-established if you re-create either module after construction, and some tools need special handling for shared tensors: safetensors refuses to save them unless deduplicated (pt8), and FSDP needs both uses wrapped in the same unit (pt11).

12. Writing a custom layer correctly: RMSNorm

Putting the rules together, here is a custom layer written the way reviewers expect. RMSNorm (dl4) divides each feature vector by its root-mean-square and multiplies by a learned per-channel gain:

class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim: int, eps: float = 1e-6):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps                                 # plain float: config, not state
        self.weight = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(dim))    # registered, trained, saved
    def forward(self, x):                              # x: (..., dim)
        xf = x.float()                                 # compute the statistic in float32
        rms = xf.pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True).add(self.eps).rsqrt()
        return (xf * rms).to(x.dtype) * self.weight
    def extra_repr(self):
        return f"{self.weight.shape[0]}, eps={self.eps}"

Each line answers one of the lesson's questions. The gain is an nn.Parameter, so it trains, moves and saves; eps is a Python float because it is configuration. The mean uses keepdim=True so it broadcasts over the last axis (pt2). The statistic is computed in float32 and cast back, because a mean of squares in bfloat16 loses precision (pt1, pt7). There is no hidden state and no mode-dependent behaviour, so train and eval give identical outputs — test that. extra_repr makes print(model) show RMSNorm(768, eps=1e-06). And it initialises its gain to 1 so that, at step 0, the layer is a pure normalisation. On 2.14 PyTorch also ships nn.RMSNorm, so in real code prefer the built-in; writing it yourself is a common interview exercise precisely because it touches registration, broadcasting and dtype at once.

13. Counting parameters, worked through for GPT-2 small

The correct count is sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) (add if p.requires_grad for trainable only). Building GPT-2 small on the meta device on 2.14 (no memory allocated) and counting gives 124,439,808 with tying and 163,037,184 without.
