deep:
__call__, hooks and why you never call forward directly

model(x) goes through nn.Module.__call__, which runs global and per-module forward pre-hooks, then forward, then forward hooks, and sets up backward hooks when any are registered. Libraries rely on this path: FSDP2 (pt11) uses pre-forward hooks to all-gather a layer's sharded parameters just before it runs and post-forward hooks to free them; activation-checkpointing wrappers and quantisation observers attach the same way; torch.compile traces through __call__. Calling model.forward(x) bypasses all of it — in a distributed model that means running on unmaterialised shards. Treat forward as an implementation detail you define but never call.

The meta device, deferred initialisation and assign=True

Constructing a 70-billion-parameter model normally allocates and randomly initialises 280 GB of float32 before you load a checkpoint that overwrites every value. The meta device avoids this: with torch.device("meta"): model = Model(cfg) creates parameters with shapes and dtypes but no storage, in milliseconds (that is how the parameter counts above were computed). You then either call model.to_empty(device="cuda") and run an init function, or load real tensors with model.load_state_dict(sd, assign=True), which replaces the meta parameters with the checkpoint's tensors instead of copying into them (copying into meta tensors is impossible). With assign=True the model adopts the checkpoint's dtype and device, so it must already be what you want. Weight tying must be re-done after assigning, since assignment replaces the shared Parameter object in one module only.

Parameter groups and what "a parameter" means to the optimiser

Optimisers receive parameters, not modules, so per-parameter policy is expressed by grouping names. The standard transformer recipe excludes biases, normalisation weights and often embeddings from weight decay: iterate over named_parameters(), put tensors with p.dim() < 2 in a group with weight_decay=0.0, and the rest in the decayed group (nanoGPT's configure_optimizers does this by dimension). Bugs appear when a parameter ends up in two groups (the optimiser raises), in no group (it is silently never trained), or when tied weights are counted twice by a name-based rule. Logging the number of tensors and elements in each group at start-up catches all three.

Re-entrancy of train(): keeping parts in eval mode

model.train() recursively sets every submodule's flag, so a frozen BatchNorm you put in eval mode is flipped back the next time the training loop calls model.train(). The robust pattern overrides train on the parent: call super().train(mode), then set the frozen submodules to eval. The same issue affects frozen encoders in multimodal models and teacher networks embedded inside a student wrapper. A related trap: requires_grad_(False) freezes weights but BatchNorm's running statistics still update in training mode, because they are buffers changed in forward, not by gradients — "frozen" BatchNorm needs both eval mode and frozen parameters.

Initialisation through the lens of signal propagation

Kaiming initialisation chooses weight variance 2/fan_in so that, for ReLU networks, each layer's output has about the same variance as its input; Xavier chooses 2/(fan_in + fan_out) for tanh-like activations. PyTorch's a = √5 default yields variance 1/(3·fan_in), smaller than Kaiming's 2/fan_in — fine for shallow networks and for architectures with normalisation layers, which rescale activations anyway. Transformers with pre-norm blocks (pt10) are robust to the exact choice inside blocks but sensitive at the edges: the embedding scale sets the initial residual stream, and the output layer's scale sets the initial loss. That is why GPT-style init is a single small standard deviation plus a residual-specific scale, and why some recent recipes (such as the μP parameterisation) scale initialisation and learning rates by width so that hyperparameters transfer across model sizes.

functional_call: running a module with someone else's parameters

torch.func.functional_call(model, params_and_buffers, args) runs a module's forward with a dictionary of tensors substituted for its registered ones, without modifying the module. It turns an nn.Module into a pure function of its parameters, which is what torch.func.grad and vmap need for per-example gradients, ensembles of models evaluated in one batched call, and meta-learning inner loops (pt14 contrasts this with JAX, where it is the only style). Tied weights complicate it: the dictionary has two names for one tensor, and if the caller supplies different values under the two names, which one should win? That is the source of the "functional_call was passed multiple values for tied weights" warning nanoGPT's author noted under torch.compile; passing tie_weights=True (the default) makes functional_call keep tied parameters tied and insist the values agree.

Buffers and distributed training

Buffers raise questions parameters do not. Under DDP (pt11), buffers such as BatchNorm statistics are broadcast from rank 0 at the start of each forward by default, so ranks agree, at a communication cost — on 2.14 the flag is forward_sync_buffers (default None, meaning True), which replaced broadcast_buffers, deprecated in 2.13; parameters instead stay in sync because their gradients are averaged. A non-persistent buffer is recomputed on every rank and never saved, which is ideal for deterministic tables such as RoPE frequencies. Mutable buffers updated in forward — running averages, step counters — are also the main obstacle to torch.compile graph capture and CUDA graphs (pt12), because they make the forward pass mutate state.
prod:
Failure mode: layers that never train

Symptom: part of the model does not change, or a newly added component has no effect. Causes: layers in a Python list or dict; a parameter created in forward; parameters replaced after the optimiser was built; an accidental detach() or no_grad in forward. Detection: after one training step, compare a checksum of every named parameter before and after (p.detach().float().sum()), and check that every parameter that should train has a non-None .grad after backward. Log len(list(model.parameters())) and the parameter count at start-up and compare with what the architecture implies.

Failure mode: the checkpoint that loads half a model

Symptom: a fine-tuned or restored model performs like a random one in some component. Cause: load_state_dict(..., strict=False) with renamed layers or a prefix mismatch (module., _orig_mod., model. from a framework wrapper), with the return value ignored. Prevention: strict loading by default; when non-strict is necessary, assert on the missing keys; keep a unit test that saves and reloads the model and compares outputs on a fixed input.

Failure mode: train/eval mode mix-ups

Symptom: validation metrics noisy or slightly off; training metrics too good after the first evaluation; results that change with evaluation batch size. Causes: evaluating without model.eval() (dropout active, BatchNorm using and updating batch statistics); never returning to train() after evaluation; a frozen BatchNorm flipped back to training mode by a later model.train(). Prevention: an evaluate() function that records was_training = model.training, calls eval(), runs under inference_mode, and restores the previous mode in a finally block.

Failure mode: initialisation at the wrong scale

Symptom: step-0 loss far above ln V, a long "hockey stick" plateau, or exploding activations in deeper models. Causes: default nn.Embedding init N(0, 1) left in place next to N(0, 0.02) weights; a custom init applied only to top-level modules (forgetting apply recurses, or calling it before submodules exist); re-initialising after loading pretrained weights. Detection: print the step-0 loss and compare with ln V; register forward hooks that log each block's output standard deviation on the first batch.

Failure mode: buffers that drift

Symptom: a model's outputs at inference slowly differ from those at the end of training, or two replicas disagree. Causes: a mutable buffer updated in forward (a running average, a step counter, a cache) that keeps changing during evaluation because the module does not check self.training; or, in multi-GPU training without buffer synchronisation, each replica's BatchNorm statistics drifting apart so the saved rank-0 copy does not represent the others. Prevention: guard buffer updates with if self.training:, keep caches that must not be saved as persistent=False, and in distributed runs keep buffer syncing on or use SyncBatchNorm.

Guard rails in CI and at start-up

Cheap automated checks catch most module bugs before they cost a training run. At start-up, log the parameter count (total and trainable), the number of tensors in each optimiser group, and the model's printed structure; compare the count with a hand calculation like the GPT-2 table in the body — a drift of exactly one layer's worth of parameters is a registration bug. In continuous integration, run a save → load → compare-outputs round trip with strict=True, a one-step training test that asserts every trainable parameter changed, and an eval-mode determinism test (two forward passes in eval mode on the same input must agree exactly, which fails if dropout is still active somewhere, for instance via a functional call). These take seconds on CPU with a tiny configuration.

The real code to compare with

nanoGPT's model.py is small enough to read in one sitting and shows every idea in this lesson in production form: a causal mask registered as a buffer for the non-flash path, the one-line tie self.transformer.wte.weight = self.lm_head.weight, self.apply(self._init_weights) followed by the residual-projection rescale "per GPT-2 paper", and a get_num_params(non_embedding=True) that subtracts position embeddings. It also records an honest note: with weight tying, torch.compile emitted a warning about "multiple values for tied weights" that the author marked as seemingly harmless — a reminder that shared parameters are a recurring edge case for tooling.
myths: Any tensor you assign in __init__ becomes part of the model.

Only nn.Parameter objects, registered buffers and nn.Module objects are registered. A plain tensor attribute is invisible to parameters(), state_dict() and .to(device): it is not saved, not loaded and stays on the CPU when the model moves to the GPU, which surfaces later as a device-mismatch error or a missing value after reload.
A Python list of layers works the same as nn.ModuleList.

A list hides the layers from nn.Module. Their parameters are not returned by parameters(), so the optimiser never updates them; they are not moved by .to(); they are absent from state_dict, so checkpoints silently omit them. The model still runs forward, which is why the bug survives until someone notices the layers never change.
eval() only matters if the model has dropout.

eval() flips the training flag on every submodule. Dropout stops dropping, BatchNorm switches from batch statistics to running statistics and stops updating them, and some modules change code paths (nn.MultiheadAttention's inference fast path, custom modules that check self.training). Forgetting it changes outputs; forgetting to switch back to train() silently disables regularisation.
Counting parameters is sum(v.numel() for v in model.state_dict().values()).

state_dict has one entry per name, and a tied weight has two names, so a tied GPT-2 small counts as 163,037,184 that way instead of 124,439,808. It also includes buffers. Use sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()), which de-duplicates shared parameters, and say whether embeddings are included.
PyTorch's default initialisation is Xavier or He initialisation.

nn.Linear and convolutions use kaiming_uniform_ with a = √5, which works out to U(−1/√fan_in, +1/√fan_in) — for a 768-input layer that is a standard deviation of about 0.021. nn.Embedding uses N(0, 1), far larger. Transformer codebases override both, typically with N(0, 0.02) and a smaller scale for residual projections, as GPT-2 and nanoGPT do.
load_state_dict() complains whenever something does not match.

Only with strict=True, the default. With strict=False it returns the missing and unexpected keys and loads the rest — and code that ignores the return value can load a checkpoint into a model where half the weights silently stay at their random initial values.
lab:
CPU, PyTorch 2.14 in gpt_env; about 15 minutes. Save as pt4_lab.py.

import math, torch, torch.nn as nn
class Buggy(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.inp = nn.Linear(8, 16)
        self.hidden = [nn.Linear(16, 16) for _ in range(3)]   # bug
        self.scale = torch.ones(16)                            # bug
        self.register_buffer("mask", torch.ones(16))
    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.inp(x)
        for layer in self.hidden: h = layer(h).relu()
        return h * self.scale * self.mask
m = Buggy()
print("registered params:", [n for n, _ in m.named_parameters()])
print("state_dict:", list(m.state_dict()))

# BatchNorm by hand
bn = nn.BatchNorm1d(2)
bn(torch.tensor([[1., 10.], [3., 30.]]))
print("running mean/var:", bn.running_mean.tolist(), bn.running_var.tolist())

# parameter count of GPT-2 small on the meta device
def block(C):
    return nn.ModuleList([nn.LayerNorm(C), nn.Linear(C, 3 * C), nn.Linear(C, C),
                          nn.LayerNorm(C), nn.Linear(C, 4 * C), nn.Linear(4 * C, C)])
with torch.device("meta"):
    wte, wpe = nn.Embedding(50257, 768), nn.Embedding(1024, 768)
    g = nn.ModuleDict(dict(wte=wte, wpe=wpe, h=nn.ModuleList(block(768) for _ in range(12)),

g.head.weight = g.wte.weight
print("params:", sum(p.numel() for p in g.parameters()))

# step-0 loss check for a small classifier
clf = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(32, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))
x, y = torch.randn(256, 32), torch.randint(0, 10, (256,))
print("loss@init:", nn.functional.cross_entropy(clf(x), y).item(), "ln 10 =", math.log(10))

  2. Running mean and variance should be [0.2, 2.0] and [1.1, 20.9] — the hand trace in the body.
  3. Params 124,439,808 and state_dict sum 163,037,184: tying counted once versus twice.
  4. loss@init should be close to 2.30. Multiply the last layer's weight by 20 under torch.no_grad() and watch the step-0 loss jump — the "init too large" signature.
recap: nn.Module's __setattr__ registers three kinds of attribute: nn.Parameter (trainable tensors), submodules, and buffers added with register_buffer; everything else is ignored by parameters(), state_dict() and .to().

Parameters require grad and are returned to optimisers; buffers are state that moves and saves with the model but is not trained, such as BatchNorm running statistics or a causal mask, and persistent=False keeps a buffer out of the state_dict.

state_dict is an ordered mapping from dotted names to tensors; load_state_dict with strict=True raises on missing or unexpected keys, and prefixes such as module. (DDP) and _orig_mod. (torch.compile) are the usual mismatch.
train() and eval() set the training flag recursively; dropout and BatchNorm read it, while autograd recording is controlled separately by no_grad or inference_mode.
Forward pre-hooks, forward hooks and full backward hooks let you inspect or modify a module's inputs, outputs and gradients without editing it, and every hook returns a handle you should remove.
Default inits are U(±1/√fan_in) for Linear and N(0, 1) for Embedding; GPT-style models use N(0, 0.02) with residual projections scaled by 1/√(2·n_layer).
Weight tying is one assignment that makes two modules share a Parameter; parameters() counts it once, state_dict lists it under both names.
GPT-2 small has 124,439,808 parameters with tying: 7,087,872 per block × 12, plus 38.6M token and 0.8M position embeddings.
Use nn.ModuleList and nn.ModuleDict for collections of layers; ModuleDict keys must be strings without dots.
glossary: A tensor registered on a module with register_buffer: it moves with .to() and is saved in the state_dict (unless persistent=False) but is not a trainable parameter.
PyTorch's data-parallel wrapper that keeps a full model copy per GPU and averages gradients between them (pt11); it stores the wrapped model as .module.
The number of inputs feeding each output unit of a layer: in_features for a linear layer, in_channels × kernel area for a convolution.
A function registered on a module that is called after its forward with (module, inputs, output), able to read or replace the output.
A function called before a module's forward with (module, inputs), able to modify the inputs.
Fully Sharded Data Parallel: splits parameters, gradients and optimiser state across GPUs; FSDP2 is the fully_shard API (pt11).
A function called during backward with the gradients with respect to a module's inputs and outputs.
Initialising weights with variance scaled by 2/fan_in (for ReLU networks) so activations neither shrink nor grow through depth.
Copy tensors from a state_dict into a module's parameters and buffers, matching by name; strict controls whether mismatched names raise.
Multi-layer perceptron; in a transformer block, the two linear layers with an activation between them (width C → 4C → C).
Containers that register the modules they hold, so their parameters are visible to the parent module.
PyTorch's base class for layers and models: it tracks parameters, buffers and submodules and provides train/eval, state_dict, hooks and device moves.
A tensor subclass that, when assigned as a module attribute, is registered as a trainable parameter with requires_grad=True.
The linear layer that computes queries, keys and values from the block input, often as one matmul producing 3·C outputs.
BatchNorm's exponential moving averages of per-channel mean and variance, updated in training mode and used in eval mode.
A dictionary from dotted names (such as blocks.0.attn.weight) to the tensors of a module's parameters and persistent buffers.
PyTorch's stateless versions of layers and losses, which take all parameters and flags as arguments.
The boolean self.training on every module, set by train() and eval(), which modules such as Dropout and BatchNorm read.
Using one parameter tensor in two places, typically the input token embedding and the output projection of a language model.
Initialising weights with variance 2/(fan_in + fan_out), designed for tanh-like activations.
drill:
Find the bug: a fine-tuning wrapper with three silent failures

This wrapper adds a classification head to a pretrained encoder and a learnable temperature. After fine-tuning, accuracy equals the baseline linear probe, the temperature never moves from 1.0, and reloading the saved checkpoint gives different predictions from the in-memory model. Find the bugs.

class Classifier(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, encoder, n_classes):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = encoder
        self.heads = {"main": nn.Linear(768, n_classes)}
        self.temp = torch.ones(1, requires_grad=True)
    def forward(self, x):
        with torch.no_grad():
            h = self.encoder(x)[:, 0]          # CLS token, (B, 768)
        return self.heads["main"](h) / self.temp

model = Classifier(encoder, 5)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=2e-5)
...
torch.save(model.state_dict(), "ckpt.pt")
Answer

Bug 1 — the head is in a plain dict. self.heads is a Python dict, so the Linear is not registered: it is not in model.parameters() (the optimiser never updates it, so the head keeps its random initial weights), it would not be moved by model.to(device), and it is not in the state_dict. On reload, a fresh randomly initialised head is created, hence different predictions. Fix: self.heads = nn.ModuleDict({"main": nn.Linear(768, n_classes)}).

Bug 2 — the temperature is a plain tensor. torch.ones(1, requires_grad=True) gets gradients but is not a registered parameter, so AdamW never sees it (it stays at 1.0), a device move would leave it behind, and it is not saved. Fix: self.temp = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(1)). (A temperature also usually wants a positive parameterisation, such as self.log_temp with exp().)

Bug 3 — no_grad around the encoder. The intent was full fine-tuning (lr 2e-5 is a fine-tuning rate), but no_grad stops all gradients into the encoder, so only the head could ever learn — which is why accuracy matches the linear probe. If freezing was intended, write it explicitly with encoder.requires_grad_(False) and exclude its parameters from the optimiser; otherwise remove the no_grad. Also check that a frozen encoder with BatchNorm or dropout is in the mode you intend. Verification after fixing: one training step should change a checksum of the encoder's, the head's and the temperature's parameters, and a save/load round trip should reproduce outputs exactly.

Estimate: what does this model cost to train?

A decoder-only model has width 2,048, 24 layers, vocabulary 32,000, tied embeddings and no biases. Estimate the parameter count and the memory for weights, gradients and AdamW states in float32.

Answer

Per block about 12·C² = 12 × 2,048² ≈ 50.3M; × 24 ≈ 1.21B. Tied embedding 32,000 × 2,048 ≈ 65.5M. Norm weights are negligible (2 × 2,048 per block). Total ≈ 1.27B parameters. At 16 bytes per parameter (FP32 weights, gradients, two Adam moments): ≈ 20.4 GB before activations — so it fits on an 80 GB GPU with room for activations, but not on a 24 GB card without sharding (pt11), mixed-precision tricks (pt7) or a lower-memory optimiser.
qa: E
What is the difference between a parameter and a buffer?

Both are tensors registered on a module that move with .to() and are saved in the state_dict. A parameter is an nn.Parameter with requires_grad=True that parameters() returns to the optimiser; a buffer is registered with register_buffer and is state that is not trained, such as BatchNorm's running mean or a precomputed causal mask. register_buffer(..., persistent=False) keeps a buffer out of the state_dict, which suits values you can recompute, like RoPE frequency tables.
E
What does model.eval() change?

It sets self.training = False on the module and every submodule. Dropout becomes the identity; BatchNorm uses its running statistics instead of the batch's and stops updating them; any custom module that checks self.training changes behaviour. It does not stop autograd recording; that needs torch.no_grad() or torch.inference_mode().

Follow-up: What happens if you call eval() and forget train() afterwards? — Training continues without dropout and with frozen BatchNorm statistics: training loss drops faster, validation gets worse, and nothing errors.
E
Why use nn.ModuleList instead of a Python list?

Because nn.Module only registers attributes that are Parameters, Modules or buffers. A list's layers are invisible: their parameters are not in parameters(), so the optimiser never updates them, they are not moved by .to(), and they are missing from the state_dict. ModuleList registers each element under an index name (blocks.0, blocks.1, …).
M
load_state_dict fails with 'Unexpected key(s): module.encoder.weight …'. What happened, and how do you fix it robustly?

The checkpoint was saved from a model wrapped in DistributedDataParallel or DataParallel, which store the real model as .module, so every key has a module. prefix. torch.compile adds _orig_mod. the same way. Fix by saving model.module.state_dict() (or the unwrapped model) in the first place, or by stripping the prefix when loading. Always inspect the incompatible keys returned by load_state_dict and fail loudly if anything important is missing.
Follow-up: Why is strict=False dangerous? — It loads what matches and silently leaves the rest at their initial values; a renamed layer produces a model that runs and is partly random.
M
What is PyTorch's default initialisation for nn.Linear, and why do transformer codebases override it?

kaiming_uniform_ with a = √5, which equals U(−1/√fan_in, +1/√fan_in); the bias uses the same bound. For fan_in 768 that is a bound of 0.036 and a standard deviation of about 0.021. Transformers override it for consistency and depth: GPT-2-style init draws all linear and embedding weights from N(0, 0.02) and scales residual output projections by 1/√(2·n_layer), so the sum of 2·n_layer residual contributions does not grow the residual stream's variance with depth. nn.Embedding's default N(0, 1) is also far too large next to 0.02 weights.

Follow-up: How do you apply a custom init to a whole model? — model.apply(fn), where fn checks isinstance(m, nn.Linear) or nn.Embedding and calls the nn.init functions, followed by a named_parameters loop for special cases such as residual projections.
M
How do you tie the input embedding and the output projection in a language model, and what changes?

Assign the same Parameter to both: lm_head.weight = wte.weight (the embedding's (V, C) weight has exactly the shape a Linear(C, V) expects). The model now has one tensor used twice; backward sums the gradients from both uses. For GPT-2 small it saves 38.6M parameters (124.4M instead of 163.0M). parameters() returns it once, state_dict lists both names, and safetensors refuses to save shared tensors unless you handle them (pt8).
M
Count the parameters of GPT-2 small (12 layers, width 768, vocabulary 50,257, context 1,024) and show your work.

Per block: two LayerNorms 2 × 1,536 = 3,072; QKV projection 768 × 2,304 + 2,304 = 1,771,776; attention output 768 × 768 + 768 = 590,592; MLP up 768 × 3,072 + 3,072 = 2,362,368; MLP down 3,072 × 768 + 768 = 2,360,064. Total 7,087,872 per block, × 12 = 85,054,464. Token embedding 50,257 × 768 = 38,597,376, position embedding 1,024 × 768 = 786,432, final LayerNorm 1,536. Sum 124,439,808 with the output head tied to the token embedding.
Follow-up: How much memory does training it with AdamW in FP32 take before activations? — About 16 bytes per parameter (weights, gradients, two Adam moments, 4 bytes each): roughly 2.0 GB.
M
How would you capture the output of every attention layer of a pretrained model without editing its code?

Register a forward hook on each attention module: for name, m in model.named_modules(): if isinstance(m, Attention): handles.append(m.register_forward_hook(lambda mod, inp, out, name=name: store.__setitem__(name, out.detach()))). Run the forward under inference_mode, then remove all handles. Detaching (and possibly moving to CPU) matters; otherwise the stored outputs keep the graph and the activations alive.
M
BatchNorm misbehaves in a fine-tuning job with batch size 2 per GPU. Why, and what are the options?

In training mode BatchNorm normalises with the current batch's mean and variance; with 2 samples those estimates are very noisy, and with 1 sample per channel it raises 'Expected more than 1 value per channel when training'. The running statistics are also updated from these noisy estimates. Options: freeze BatchNorm (keep those layers in eval mode and their parameters frozen), use SyncBatchNorm to compute statistics across GPUs, or replace it with GroupNorm or LayerNorm, which do not depend on the batch.

Follow-up: How do you keep BatchNorm in eval mode while the rest trains? — Override the model's train() to call super().train(mode) and then set bn modules to eval(), because a later model.train() would otherwise flip them back.
H
Explain what happens inside nn.Module when you write self.proj = nn.Linear(768, 768).

nn.Module overrides __setattr__. When the value is a Module it is stored in self._modules under 'proj'; a Parameter goes to self._parameters; a tensor registered via register_buffer goes to self._buffers. parameters(), named_modules(), state_dict(), .to(), train()/eval() and apply() all walk these dictionaries recursively, building dotted names like blocks.3.proj.weight. Plain attributes go into the normal __dict__ and are invisible to all of that, which is why a plain tensor attribute is not moved or saved.
Follow-up: How do you make a non-Parameter tensor follow the module across devices without saving it? — register_buffer(name, t, persistent=False).
H
A colleague's custom module works on CPU but fails on GPU with 'Expected all tensors to be on the same device'. What do you look for?

A tensor created in __init__ as a plain attribute (self.scale = torch.ones(C)) — not registered, so model.to('cuda') leaves it on the CPU — or a tensor created inside forward with a factory function and no device (torch.arange(T) instead of torch.arange(T, device=x.device)). Fix by registering it as a buffer or Parameter, and by creating tensors in forward with device=x.device and dtype=x.dtype (or torch.*_like).
H
How do initialisation choices show up in the first training steps, and how do you verify an initialisation is right?

At initialisation the output logits should be small so the loss starts near ln(V) for a V-way classifier (ln 50,257 ≈ 10.8 for GPT-2's vocabulary); a much larger starting loss means the output layer or embeddings are initialised too large, producing confident random predictions and a 'hockey stick' loss curve. Verify by checking the step-0 loss, the standard deviation of activations at each layer (forward hooks) — they should stay roughly constant through depth — and the gradient norms per layer. Karpathy's Recipe lists 'verify loss @ init' as a first step for exactly this reason.

Follow-up: Why does the residual scaling 1/√(2·n_layer) help? — Each block adds two contributions to the residual stream; without scaling, the stream's variance grows linearly with depth, so later layers see ever larger inputs and the output layer starts far from small logits.
